title: The Gibraltar Deal: Open Borders, Sovereignty and Spain's Role
label: 15 September 2026 · UK–EU agreement on Gibraltar
summary: The House of Lords European Affairs Committee questioned UK ministers and officials about a new agreement designed to keep Gibraltar's border with Spain open after Brexit. The agreement protects the daily movement of around 15,000 people, creates new arrangements for trade and immigration, and aims to give businesses long-term certainty. The Government insisted that Gibraltar remains fully under British sovereignty and that its people chose the arrangements. Several committee members challenged that position, arguing that Spain and the EU now have significant practical powers over Gibraltar's borders, trade and immigration. The hearing also examined protections for British military operations, who can refuse entry to Gibraltar, how the agreement will be funded, and whether Spain could eventually bring it to an end. Ministers presented the deal as a lasting settlement, although important questions about entry decisions and the agreement's termination remained unresolved.

glossary.definition: A group of European countries that generally allow people to travel between them without routine passport checks at their shared borders.
An EU system that electronically records when certain travellers from outside the EU enter or leave the Schengen area.
An arrangement in which participating territories remove certain trade barriers between them and apply common tariffs to goods arriving from elsewhere.
A trade agreement between countries around the Pacific and elsewhere that sets rules for trading goods and services.
Additional sections attached to a legal agreement that provide detailed rules, lists or supporting information.
Rules made through the European Union's legal system that apply to its members and sometimes to other places through agreements.
A way of settling disagreements by asking an independent panel to consider the dispute and make a decision.
The court responsible for interpreting EU law and ensuring it is applied consistently.
The usual limit allowing many non-EU visitors to spend up to 90 days in the Schengen area during any rolling 180-day period.
A political agreement setting out how two governments will work together, without necessarily creating legally enforceable obligations.
A joint body established by the agreement where representatives can oversee its operation and address problems.
A treaty provision setting out what happens if Gibraltar refuses to follow an update to EU rules it has agreed to apply.
A treaty provision setting out the ordinary procedure for ending the agreement.

chapters.title: Why Gibraltar needed a separate agreement
chapters.takeaway: Temporary arrangements kept Gibraltar's border functioning after Brexit, but a lasting agreement was needed to protect jobs and avoid costly disruption.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Why wasn't Gibraltar included in the UK's trade agreement with the EU in 2020? We've relied on temporary arrangements ever since. Why weren't they enough, and why has it taken five years to reach this agreement?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: My understanding is that the EU wanted Gibraltar dealt with separately, probably because Spain believed it needed different arrangements from the rest of the UK. The previous Government accepted that approach. Looking back, I'm not sure the detailed border arrangements we've now negotiated could have been agreed alongside the much wider UK–EU trade deal.

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: The main objective was always to keep the border between Gibraltar and Spain open and easy to cross. Gibraltar's economy depends heavily on people travelling across it for work. Without an agreement, disruption to workers, trade and investment could have cost hundreds of millions of pounds. That would have affected communities on both sides.

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: The temporary arrangements worked reasonably well. They depended on informal understandings between Gibraltar, the UK and Spain. Most importantly, they allowed EU and Gibraltar residents to cross the land border without routine immigration checks. There were also arrangements covering healthcare and the protection of personal information.

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: But there were growing difficulties, particularly for some groups such as defence personnel. More fundamentally, businesses couldn't plan confidently when everything depended on goodwill. Political changes could overturn those understandings. The EU's new entry/exit system also meant Spain couldn't continue the existing border arrangements indefinitely.

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: The negotiations took so long because the issues were exceptionally complicated. We needed detailed solutions for airport checks, customs, military activity and new physical facilities. There were also political interruptions, including upheaval in Britain in 2022, Spanish elections in 2023 and a change of British Government in 2024.

turns.speaker: Lord Jackson of Peterborough
turns.text: You keep talking about making the border easy to cross. How is that different from giving people unrestricted freedom to move between Gibraltar and Spain?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: What we're talking about is the practical ability of roughly 15,000 people who cross the land border every day to do so without checks. That movement is essential to Gibraltar's economy. There are different arrangements for people arriving by air or sea. Keeping the land border open was the particular outcome Gibraltar wanted.

turns.speaker: Baroness Suttie
turns.text: What was the biggest problem Brexit created for Gibraltar that this agreement needed to solve?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: The biggest danger was the introduction of full immigration checks at the land border. Gibraltar's Government made clear that this would be disastrous for the territory and the surrounding region. The temporary arrangements prevented that for a while, but only a binding agreement could provide the long-term security people needed.

chapters.title: Sovereignty, trade and Spain's influence
chapters.takeaway: The Government insisted that British sovereignty remains untouched, while committee members questioned whether Gibraltar has surrendered important practical powers.

turns.speaker: Lord Grantchester
turns.text: This agreement involves the UK, the EU, Gibraltar and Spain. Gibraltar will also have to keep certain rules in line with EU rules as they change. How will the Government manage all those relationships? Will it need more diplomatic staff?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: The agreement creates a co-operation council led by ministers, three specialist committees and procedures for settling disagreements. There will also be working groups involving the UK and Spain. Our officials in London, Gibraltar, Madrid and Brussels will continue working with the relevant governments. It's a complicated arrangement, but we don't expect it to require a significant increase in resources.

turns.speaker: Baroness Ashton of Upholland
turns.text: British sovereignty over Gibraltar has always been a central concern. Did the negotiations force you to compromise any important principles? Are you confident the agreement protects sovereignty completely?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: Yes. Sovereignty wasn't discussed as something to be transferred, and the agreement doesn't change it. Article 2 explicitly says the treaty cannot affect or be used to challenge the existing position on sovereignty. These are practical arrangements governing Gibraltar's relationship with the EU, not a transfer of territory or sovereignty.

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: Some of the practical arrangements differ from what was originally envisaged. But Gibraltar's Government chose them, and its Parliament supported the agreement unanimously. The UK has followed the principle that decisions about Gibraltar shouldn't be made without Gibraltar's agreement.

turns.speaker: Lord Moynihan of Chelsea
turns.text: But isn't Gibraltar effectively being taken out of Britain's independent trade policy? Could Gibraltar still join the CPTPP trade agreement, for example? Surely losing that freedom is a meaningful restriction on sovereignty.

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: I don't agree that sovereignty is affected. Gibraltar made choices about its trading arrangements to protect the open border and its economy. Governments regularly accept particular rules through international agreements in return for benefits.

turns.speaker: Paul Hughes
turns.text: The new customs union arrangement with the EU concerns goods, such as physical products crossing borders. Gibraltar's main international trading interests are in services, such as financial and professional services. Gibraltar could participate in the services part of CPTPP, but not its arrangements for goods.

turns.speaker: Lord Moynihan of Chelsea
turns.text: But that confirms my concern. Britain has deliberately chosen not to join the EU's customs union, while Gibraltar will now be in a customs union with the EU for goods. That limits the trade policies Gibraltar can follow.

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: There's an important distinction. Gibraltar isn't joining the EU customs union outright. It has negotiated its own specific customs union arrangement with the EU for goods. That's a choice its Government made.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Even if sovereignty hasn't formally been transferred, Spanish customs and police officers now have roles under the agreement. What's to stop Spain gradually increasing its authority within Gibraltar?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: The agreement carefully limits what each Spanish authority can do. Spanish military officers, for example, have a narrow role involving special arrangements for defence personnel and limited information sharing. They don't gain broader authority over British military operations. More practical co-operation with Spanish police and military officials is desirable, but that isn't the same as giving them unrestricted powers.

turns.speaker: Lord Jackson of Peterborough
turns.text: I remain concerned. The treaty has 43 annexes, and Gibraltar must continue following certain EU rules as they change. It also gives Spain substantial powers affecting arrests, searches, residence permits, security decisions and entry into Gibraltar. How can you be certain that these arrangements don't seriously reduce British sovereignty?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: I reject the suggestion that sovereignty has been reduced. Also, it isn't correct that all 43 annexes impose EU law. Most concern other matters, such as procedures or lists of offences. We estimate that around eight contain references to EU law. Gibraltar has agreed to follow those particular rules because doing so brings the benefits of an open border.

turns.speaker: Lord Jackson of Peterborough
turns.text: Whether Gibraltar's Government agreed is a separate question from whether a British territory has lost powers. You can't answer every concern about sovereignty simply by saying Gibraltar consented.

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: I understand the distinction you're making, but I don't accept your conclusion. Gibraltar has chosen a limited set of arrangements suited to its circumstances. It hasn't been required to adopt large amounts of unrelated EU law. The agreement protects the border and the economy while leaving sovereignty unchanged.

turns.speaker: Lord Jackson of Peterborough
turns.text: There's also concern that Spain and the EU could use their powers to prevent British nationals from entering to work, potentially favouring Spanish workers. Even if those powers aren't exercised, doesn't their existence create a problem?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: I don't recognise that description of the agreement. Gibraltar already depends heavily on workers coming from Spain, which is why keeping the border open matters. Gibraltar remains responsible for deciding who can enter. Economic changes may cause concerns, but the treaty hasn't fundamentally changed that relationship. It's given people greater legal certainty.

chapters.title: Who decides who can enter Gibraltar?
chapters.takeaway: Gibraltar formally controls admission to its territory, but its decision to recognise certain Spanish security refusals creates difficult practical questions.

turns.speaker: Lord Brennan of Canton
turns.text: Let's look at what happens when someone arrives at Gibraltar Airport. Who actually decides whether they're allowed in? Can Spanish officials stop someone entering Gibraltar?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: Gibraltar remains responsible for entry into its territory. Its residents always have the right to return home. Other arrivals now go through two checks: first with Gibraltar's immigration officers, then with Spanish officials checking whether they can enter the Schengen area. Passing both checks allows someone to enter Gibraltar and travel into that wider area.

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: Spain can refuse someone entry into the Schengen area if they don't meet its requirements, including where there's a security alert. Gibraltar's Government has voluntarily decided to recognise Spanish refusal decisions based on security or public safety concerns when making its own entry decisions.

turns.speaker: Lord Brennan of Canton
turns.text: So although you say Gibraltar makes the final decision, a Spanish security refusal could effectively prevent someone entering Gibraltar?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: The distinction is important. Spain decides whether someone can enter the Schengen area. Gibraltar decides whether they can enter Gibraltar. But Gibraltar has chosen to recognise the relevant Spanish decisions. That's the arrangement its Government agreed to.

turns.speaker: Lord Brennan of Canton
turns.text: And in practice, Gibraltar has agreed to follow those Spanish security decisions?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: Yes, that's the principle of recognising each other's decisions that Gibraltar has chosen.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What about the opposite situation? Suppose Gibraltar refuses someone entry but Spain wants to admit them. Does Gibraltar's decision prevent them travelling into Spain?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: Gibraltar can refuse entry to anyone who isn't a Gibraltar resident, including British nationals. The decision about entry into Gibraltar remains Gibraltar's.

turns.speaker: Paul Hughes
turns.text: Everyone goes through both sets of checks. There are also rights that must be respected. Gibraltar residents can't be prevented from returning home, and the same principle applies to Spanish residents. Spain could allow someone into the Schengen area even if Gibraltar refused them entry into Gibraltar.

turns.speaker: Lord Brennan of Canton
turns.text: But what if that person is from another EU country, or somewhere outside the EU? Could they still pass through Gibraltar to get home?

turns.speaker: Paul Hughes
turns.text: I think the same principle would apply and they could travel through to return home, but I'd need to check the exact position.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: That's precisely the difficulty. If Gibraltar says no and Spain says yes, what actually happens to the person? We need to understand how those conflicting decisions are handled, including whether the rules differ according to nationality.

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: That conflict is theoretically possible. We don't have a complete answer for you today, but we'll clarify the position and come back to the committee.

chapters.title: Protecting the military base and settling disputes
chapters.takeaway: The agreement gives British defence personnel special border arrangements and protects UK military control, while allowing limited EU involvement in interpreting agreed rules.

turns.speaker: The Duke of Wellington
turns.text: Will this agreement affect access to Gibraltar's British naval and military facilities? Could it interfere with the movement of personnel or with military operations?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: Protecting the UK's independent control of its military facilities was an absolute requirement throughout negotiations. Spain has no power to approve or control British military operations, deployments or movements. The agreement preserves our ability to use and supply the base.

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: Military personnel, civilians on defence business, their immediate families and certain defence partners are exempt from routine Schengen entry and exit checks. There are also special arrangements for military supplies and equipment that can have both military and civilian uses. We share limited information with Spanish military officers to make these arrangements work, but they don't control our operations.

turns.speaker: The Duke of Wellington
turns.text: Are the local British military commanders satisfied? Could the arrangements actually improve the situation?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: Yes. I spoke to the Commander British Forces Gibraltar, who was positive about the early experience and the relationship developing with Spanish counterparts. The agreement has only been operating provisionally for about two months, but the early signs are encouraging.

turns.speaker: Baroness Smith of Newnham
turns.text: You say military personnel and their families are exempt from routine checks. What happens if they travel elsewhere in the Schengen area? Normally many British visitors are limited by the 90-day rule. How will officers prove their special status and avoid problems?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: They can show documents establishing their eligibility, such as identity documents or official military movement orders. There's also a system for recording when the Schengen time restrictions apply to them and when they don't. That has been improved during the first months of the agreement.

turns.speaker: Lord Tugendhat
turns.text: I'm interested in how disagreements under this agreement will be settled. Could the arrangement provide a model for other agreements Britain is negotiating with the EU, particularly where we agree to follow some EU rules without joining the EU's wider systems?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: There are certainly parallels. Gibraltar has accepted particular rules to secure practical benefits, and we're discussing similar choices in other negotiations with the EU. I don't know enough about the detailed dispute procedure to say how far it could serve as a model, so I'll ask Paul to explain.

turns.speaker: Paul Hughes
turns.text: Most of the arbitration process is fairly standard. The unusual part concerns disagreements over the meaning of EU law. Those questions can be referred to the European Court of Justice. This approach was also used in the UK's withdrawal agreement with the EU and earlier European agreements. It might provide a basis for other negotiations, although officials handling those discussions would need to answer that.

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: To be clear, the European Court of Justice's role is to explain what EU law means where Gibraltar has agreed to apply it. It isn't being given a general power to decide every dispute under the treaty.

chapters.title: Costs and the UK–Gibraltar partnership
chapters.takeaway: Gibraltar will fund the UK's contribution to a new regional funding arrangement, while a separate political agreement sets out how the two governments will work together.

turns.speaker: Lord Elliott of Mickle Fell
turns.text: The treaty proposes a financial arrangement to support economic development across Gibraltar and the surrounding Spanish region. How much will Gibraltar pay, and will British taxpayers have to contribute?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: The aim is to help the whole region benefit from easier movement of people and goods. The two sides will establish separate funds. Gibraltar's fund might, for example, pay for training and development for workers who cross the border. The detailed plans and timetable haven't yet been settled.

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: Importantly, the UK's contribution to this arrangement will be funded by Gibraltar, under our separate agreement with its Government. It won't come from UK taxpayers.

turns.speaker: Lord Barrow
turns.text: Gibraltar's Parliament supported the treaty unanimously in March 2026, but that support depended on a separate agreement with the UK, known as a concordat. Why was that needed, and what difference does it make?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: The concordat explains how the British and Gibraltar Governments will work together to carry out the treaty. It sets out their responsibilities while respecting Gibraltar's control over its own affairs and the UK's international obligations. Gibraltar wanted that clarity, and we consider it an essential part of making the treaty work over the long term.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: But what's its legal status? Is the concordat enforceable in the same way as the treaty?

turns.speaker: Paul Hughes
turns.text: No. It's a political agreement between the British and Gibraltar Governments.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: That's an important distinction. The treaty creates legal obligations and procedures for enforcing them. The concordat depends on the two governments continuing to cooperate. Political priorities could change, so it can't provide the same guarantees.

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: That's true, but both governments have strong reasons to keep the relationship working. Gibraltar needs clarity about how the treaty will operate, and the UK has every reason to maintain good relations with Gibraltar. I'm hopeful the concordat will continue to guide us.

turns.speaker: Lord Barrow
turns.text: I'd describe it as an ongoing conversation between the British and Gibraltar authorities about how the agreement works.

chapters.title: Could Spain bring the agreement to an end?
chapters.takeaway: The agreement is intended to last, but it contains several possible routes to termination, including a Spanish role after a four-year review that officials could not fully clarify.

turns.speaker: Lord Moynihan of Chelsea
turns.text: I want to understand how this treaty can be ended. There seem to be three routes. As I read Article 334, the normal process requires 12 months' notice, Gibraltar's consent and a referendum. But Article 19.5 appears to allow termination after 90 days. And another provision seems to let Spain bring about the agreement's termination. Doesn't that create serious uncertainty?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: Article 19.5 is much more specific than that suggests. It deals with the situation where Gibraltar rejects or ignores an update to EU rules that it has already agreed to follow. That starts a 90-day period during which the parties try to find an alternative solution. The intention is to resolve the disagreement, not to make ending the treaty easy. Similar provisions exist in EU agreements with Norway, Switzerland and Iceland.

turns.speaker: Paul Hughes
turns.text: The Spanish provision is different. My understanding is that, after a review of the rules governing people's movement at the end of four years, Spain can tell the EU that it is no longer satisfied. The EU would then begin a process to end the treaty. There would be a period, possibly nine months, in which the parties could seek alternatives.

turns.speaker: Paul Hughes
turns.text: That reflects the reality that Spain is responsible for putting much of the EU side of this agreement into practice. On our side, the concordat sets out how Britain would approach decisions about termination. Both arrangements recognise that the treaty is primarily about the relationship between Gibraltar and Spain.

turns.speaker: Lord Moynihan of Chelsea
turns.text: But circumstances can change dramatically. Gibraltar may strongly support the agreement now, and Spain may currently cooperate, but future governments could think differently. We shouldn't assume these termination provisions will never be used simply because everyone is satisfied today.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: I want to be absolutely clear about Spain's power. Can Spain demand that the EU end the treaty whenever it wishes, or only after the four-year review?

turns.speaker: Paul Hughes
turns.text: It's not a power Spain can exercise at any time. My understanding is that it arises through the specific review of the arrangements for people's movement after four years.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: And is that a one-off opportunity at the four-year point, rather than something Spain can use repeatedly?

turns.speaker: Paul Hughes
turns.text: I'm fairly certain that's correct, but I would want that confirmed.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Please come back to us with a definite answer. That distinction is important.

turns.speaker: Lord Tugendhat
turns.text: Gibraltar has been the subject of negotiations and disagreements for many years. Do you believe this agreement finally settles the major issues, or should we expect more negotiations?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: As far as the treaty is concerned, I believe this settles the outstanding issues from Brexit. We've achieved a lasting arrangement while protecting British sovereignty completely. There will certainly be practical adjustments as the new arrangements operate, including in economic activity and cooperation between different authorities. But those are questions of making the agreement work, rather than reopening its foundations. I believe it gives Gibraltar a stable basis for its relationship with the EU for many years.
